newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian steel mill management suffers setback.
newsitem.headline: Russian steel mill management suffers setback.

text.p: The management of a Russian steel plant, locked in a war with foreigners over board representation, admitted partial defeat on Tuesday when it said shareholders had rejected a new charter.

The management-sponsored charter would have served as the legal basis for the current board of the Novolipetsk plant to govern until new elections, effectively excluding the outside shareholders who claim a controlling stake.
No date has been set for new elections, so approval of the charter, discussed at a shareholders' meeting on Saturday, might have been regarded as acceptance of the status quo.

"The new version of the charter was not approved at the meeting," Novolipetsk Steel Plant, one of Russia's two top steel producers, said in a news release issued on Tuesday by the company, based 400 km (250 miles) south of Moscow.

Lawyers for the foreign shareholders said they would soon call a new meeting to elect a fresh board of directors, although the current management will continue to run the plant despite the lack of a new charter.
The two groups have been battling in court for months in a critical attempt by outsiders to challenge management and force reform using the Russian legal system.

But the system is ill-equipped to deal with such issues since the Federal Commission for the Securities Market, the federal markets watchdog, does not have authority to enforce joint stock company, or corporate, law.
Outsiders hold at least 50 percent of most large companies, a securities commission spokesman has said.

Lawyers for Cambridge Capital Management, which along with the Sputnik Fund and Russia's Bank MFK is requesting board representation of Novolipetsk, said rejection of the charter meant management had no legal authority to act.
The three claim over 50 percent of Novolipetsk shares.
"The company now works without any charter," said Chadbourne & Parke lawyer Mikhail Rozenberg, adding that Cambridge expected to request a new shareholders meeting after a court case on July 23.
"If the company does not carry out such a meeting, it could be liable for criminal charges for not carrying out the court decision," he said.
Novolipetsk directors say they have acted within the law.

The annual report said Novolipetsk's profits fell to 700 billion roubles ($121.3 million) in 1996 from three trillion roubles in 1995, though the type of profit and accounting methods were not specified.
It said first half steel production this year had risen six percent on the same period a year ago to 3.46 million tonnes and 1996 production was unchanged from 1995 at 7.06 million tonnes.
Rolled steel, Novolipetsk's main product, rose five percent in the first half to 3.31 million tonnes from 3.14 and four percent in 1996 to 6.52 million tonnes.
Exports of all products rose to 77 percent of production from 52 percent, though it was unclear if that was calculated by steel output or value of sales.
